'''bravura''' (brȧ-vö′rä), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [It., bravery, spirit, < ''bravo'': see ''brave.''] '''I.''' ''n.'' In ''music'', a florid air, requiring great force and spirit in the performer, and serving to display his or her power, flexibility of voice, and distinctness of articulation.

'''II.''' ''a.'' In ''music'', spirited; florid; brilliant: as, a ''bravura'' air: chiefly applied to vocal compositions, but occasionally to instrumental.

'''braw''' (brâ), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Sc.: see ''brave.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Brave; fine; gay; handsome; pleasant; agreeable; worthy; excellent; stout: as, a ''braw'' new gown; a ''braw'' man; ''braw'' lads and bonny lasses. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|There’s ''braw'', ''braw'' lads on Yarrow braes.
{{right|''Burns'', Gala Water.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n. pl.'' One’s best apparel; finery.

'''brawd†''', ''v. t.'' See ''broud'', ''broid.''

'''brawdery†''', ''n.'' An obsolete variant of ''broidery.''

'''brawet''' (brou′et), ''n.'' A young eel. Also written ''brawat.'' [North. Eng.]

'''brawl<sup>1</sup>''' (brâl), ''v.'' [Early mod. E. also ''brall'', < ME. ''brallen'', cry out, vociferate, = D. ''brallen'', boast, = Dan. ''bralle'', jabber, chatter, = MHG. ''prālen'', G. ''prahlen'', boast, vaunt, flaunt; apparently identical with ME. ''brawlen'', ''braulen'', quarrel, W. ''brawl'', a boast, ''brolio'', boast, vaunt, ''bragal'', vociferate, etc. Cf. also F. ''brailler'' (= Pr. ''brailar''), cry out, bawl, prob. < ''braire'', bray: see

'''Brauronian''' (brâ-rō′ni-an), ''a.''   [< Gr. Βραυρωνία, of Brauron, an epithet of Artemis, < Βραυρών, an Attic village and deme near Marathon.]   Of or relating to Brauron, a deme of Attica, or to its inhabitants; specifically, an epithet of Artemis, who was worshiped under this title on the Acropolis of Athens.

'''brava''' (brä′vä). See remarks under ''bravo, interj.''

'''bravade†''' (brạ-vād′), ''n.''   [< F. ''bravade'': see ''bravado.'']   Same as ''bravado.''
{{smaller block|<poem>The great Pacheco, like himself, this hot
And fierce ''bravade'' shall in a trice make vain.</poem>
{{right|''Fanshawe.''}}}}

'''bravado''' (bra-vā′dō), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Formerly also ''bravade'' (< F. ''bravade'') = ODan. ''bravat'', < Sp. ''bravada'', now ''bravata'' (= It. ''bravata''), boast, vain ostentation, < ''bravo'' = F. ''brave'' = It. ''bravo'', brave, bullying: see ''brave'' and ''bravo.'']   '''I.''' ''n.''; pl. ''bravados'' or ''bravadoes'' (-dōz). '''1.''' Pretentious boldness or bravery; arrogant or boastful menace; swaggering defiance.
{{smaller block|In spite of our host’s ''bravado.'' {{right|''Irving.''}}}}
{{smaller block|No sooner was this mad ''bravado'' agreed upon than they turned the reins of their horses and made for Seville.
{{right|''Irving'', Moorish Chronicle, p. 109.}}}}
'''2†.''' One who indulges in boastful and arrogant menaces.
{{smaller block|The hectors and ''bravadoes'' of the House, who show all the zeal on this occasion. {{right|''Pepys'', Diary, Feb. 28, 1667.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Arrogantly bold or menacing; said or done in bravado: as, “''bravado'' bets,” ''Disraeli'', {{smaller|Coningsby, v. 5.}}

'''bravado''' (bra-vä′dō), ''v. i.''   [< ''bravado'', ''n.'']   To act in a spirit of bravado; storm; rage. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Like winds where Æolus ''bravado’d.'' {{right|''Lloyd'', The Poet.}}}}

'''bravaisite''' (bra-vā′zīt), ''n.''   [< ''Bravais'', a French crystallographer, + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.]   A hydrous silicate of aluminium with small amounts of iron, calcium, magnesium, and potassium, occurring in crystalline fibrous forms in the coal-measures of Noyant, in Maine-et-Loire, France.

'''brave''' (brāv), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [First in early mod. E.; = G. ''brav'' (17th century) = MD. ''brauwe'', ''braue'', fine, gallant (in appearance), ''brave'', fierce, also fine, gallant (Kilian), mod. D. ''braaf'', brave, gallant, courageous (cf. MD. ''brauwen'', adorn, ''braveren'', be fierce, = MLG. ''bravēren'' = ODan. ''bravere'', strut), = Dan. ''brav'', brave, worthy, = OSw. ''braf'', Sw. ''bra'', good, > prob. Sc. ''braw'', good, also pleasant, fine, handsome, etc., < F. ''brave'', brave, fine, gallant, etc., introduced in the 16th century, < It. ''bravo'', brave, hardy, OIt. tempestuous (cf. ''bravo'', ''n.'', cutthroat, assassin, bravo), = Sp. Pg. ''bravo'', brave, etc., = Pr. ''brau'', fem. ''brava'', brave, hard, wicked, etc. (ML. ''bravus'', a bravo, cutthroat); perhaps = OF. *''brou'' in ''rabroüer'', check, chide, etc., ''brouaz'', ''brouhaha'', a bluster, ''brouhoux'', storms, blusters, etc., ''brouée'', blustering. Origin and relations uncertain. There appear to be at least two words confused: in the sense ‘fine, good,’ etc., cf. Bret. ''brav'', ''brao'', fine, agreeable, pretty, ''braga'', strut, dress in fine clothes (see ''brag''); in the sense ‘bold, wild,’ etc., cf. OF. ''braou'', ''brau'', ML. ''bravus'', ''bravis'', a young untamed ox, OIt. ''bravo'', tempestuous, Sp. ''brava'', a heavy swell of the sea, OF. *''brou'' (above), etc.; W. ''braw'', terror, fright.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Possessing or exhibiting courage or courageous endurance; intrepid; valiant; fearless: as, a ''brave'' warrior; a ''brave'' act; he was ''brave'' under calamity.
{{smaller block|<poem>Two ''braver'' men
Ne’er spurr’d their coursers at the trumpet’s sound.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., v. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''brave'' man is not he who feels no fear, . . .
But he whose noble mind its fears subdues.</poem>
{{right|''J. Baillie'', Basil.}}}}
{{smaller block|The coward sneaks to death, the ''brave'' live on.
{{right|''Dr. Sewell'', The Suicide, ii. 55.}}}}
'''2.''' Making a fine display in bearing, dress, or appearance generally; having a noble mien: said of persons.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have gold, and therefore will be ''brave'',
In silks I’ll rattle it of every colour.</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', Tu Quoque, vii.}}}}
'''3.''' Splendid; beautiful; gorgeous; gaudy: said of things.
{{smaller block|With blossoms ''brave'' bedecked daintily.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. vii. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|And wear my dagger with the ''braver'' grace.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|He had them into the very best room in the house (a very ''brave'' room it was).
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, p. 252.}}}}
'''4.''' Excellent; capital; fine; admirable. {{smaller|[Formerly in very common use in this sense as a general term}} of commendation; often also used ironically; now obsolete except perhaps in irony.]

{{smaller block|Iron is a ''brave'' commodity where wood aboundeth.
{{right|''Bacon.''}}}}

{{smaller block|I’ll devise thee ''brave'' punishments for him.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 4.}}}}

{{smaller block|='''Syn. 1.''' ''Gallant, Valiant, Courageous, Brave, Heroic,'' valorous, dauntless, chivalrous, doughty, resolute, manful. ''Gallant'', splendid in dress or qualities, is most appropriately used with regard to courage which exhibits itself in deeds attracting attention and applause; of the first four words it is that which may have in it most of compliment and least of high commendation, but it is often a strong word, expressing splendid bravery in action: as, he was a ''gallant'' officer. ''Valiant'' is also brave in action, especially in opposing physical force, as in battle. The word is now elevated and poetic. ''Courageous'' denotes the possession of that spirit which enables one fearlessly and with full presence of mind to face danger. ''Brave'' is the most comprehensive of the words; it may denote the possession of the highest and noblest kind of courage and fortitude, of that spirit which enables a man to bear up against evil and danger, as well as to go forth to face it. ''Courageous'' has much of this breadth of meaning, but is applicable rather to doing than to enduring; ''brave'' is both passive and active. ''Heroic'' combines the meaning of all the other words in the superlative degree. It indicates a lofty superiority to fear, a noble self-forgetfulness, an almost superhuman power to dare, achieve, or suffer. It bears the same relation to the other words that ''sublime'' bears to ''great'', ''grand'', or ''lofty''.}}

{{smaller block|The Sardinian fleet had been withdrawn from Venice, and the ''gallant'' resistance of the Venetians was fast drawing to a close.
{{right|''E. Dicey'', Victor Emmanuel, p. 108.}}}}

{{smaller block|Plague on’t; an I thought he had been ''valiant'' and so cunning in fence, I’d have seen him damned ere I’d have challenged him.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4.}}}}

<poem>But he rose upon their decks, and he cried:
“I have fought for Queen and Faith like a ''valiant'' man and true.”</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', The Revenge.}}}}

{{smaller block|Only be thou strong and very ''courageous'', that thou mayest observe to do according to all the law which Moses my servant commanded thee.
{{right|Josh. i. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But, what with pleasure Heaven itself surveys,
A ''brave'' man struggling in the storms of fate,
And greatly falling with a falling state.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Prol. to Cato, l. 31.}}}}
'''II.''' ''n.'' [Cf. ''bravo'', ''n.''] '''1.''' A brave, bold, or daring person; a man daring beyond discretion. Specifically—'''2.''' A North American Indian or other savage warrior: as, the chief was accompanied by two hundred ''braves''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Two from among them [Indian warriors] advancing,
Came to parley with Standish, and offer him furs as a present; . . .
''Braves'' of the tribe were these, and brothers gigantic in stature.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Courtship of Miles Standish, vii.}}}}
{{smaller block|With three strokes to each, the scalps of the victims being suddenly taken off, the ''brave'' flies back with his companions, to hang the trophies in his cabin.
{{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. U. S., II. 431.}}}}
'''3†.''' A hector; a bully; a bravo.
{{smaller block|Too insolent, too much a ''brave''. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''4†.''' [< ''brave'', ''v.''] A boast; a challenge; a defiance.
{{smaller block|<poem>I will not bear these ''braves'' of thine.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis time
To be avenged on you for all your ''braves''.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe'', Edward II., iii. 3.}}}}

'''brave''' (brāv), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''braved'', ppr. ''braving''.   [< F. ''braver'', brave, affront, defy, etc., < ''brave'', brave.]   '''1.''' To encounter with courage and fortitude; set at defiance; defy; challenge; dare.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ills of love, not those of fate, I fear;</poem>}}

{{smaller block|These I can ''brave'', but those I cannot bear. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

{{smaller block|Louis the Fifteenth ''braved'' the hatred and contempt of his subjects during many years of the most odious and imbecile misgovernment.
{{right|''Macaulay'', West. Rev. Defence of Mill.}}}}

'''2†.''' To wear a boasting appearance of.

{{smaller block|To ''brave'' that which they believe not. {{right|''Bacon'', Essays.}}}}

<poem>Another,
Reputed valiant, lives by the sword, and takes up
Quarrels, or ''braves'' them, as the novice likes,
To gild his reputation.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Ford'', Fancies, i. 3.}}}}

'''3†.''' To make fine, showy, or splendid. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|He [the sun] should have ''brav’d'' the east an hour ago.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., v. 3.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To brave out''', to face out; brazen out: generally with an indefinite ''it'' as object.}}

{{smaller block|However we ''brave it out'', we men are a little breed.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, iv.}}}}

'''bravely''' (brāv′li), ''adv.'' In a brave manner. {{smaller|(''a'') Courageously; gallantly; splendidly; heroically.}}

{{smaller block|Who combats ''bravely'' is not therefore brave.
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, i. 115.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') Finely; gaudily.}}

{{smaller block|And decked herself ''bravely'', to allure the eyes of all men that should see her. {{right|Judith x. 4.}}}}

{{smaller|(''c'') Well; prosperously: as, he is getting on ''bravely''.}}

{{smaller block|The tug was towing ''bravely''.
{{right|''W. C. Russell'', Jack’s Courtship, xxi.}}}}

'''braveness†''' (brāv′nes), ''n.'' The quality of being brave; bravery: as, “the ''braveness'' of the exploit,” ''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 306.

'''bravery''' (brā′vėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''braveries'' (-iz).   [< F. ''braverie'', gallantry, splendor, etc., < ''brave'', brave: see ''brave'' and ''-ery''.]   '''1.''' The quality of being brave; courage; heroism; undaunted spirit; intrepidity; gallantry; fearlessness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Remember, sir, my liege, . . .
The natural ''bravery'' of your isle.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Lancelot, the flower of ''bravery''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
'''2.''' Showiness; splendor; magnificence.
{{smaller block|The ''bravery'' of their tinkling ornaments. {{right|Is. iii. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|Great ''bravery'' of building, to the marvellous beautifying of the realm. {{right|''Camden.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>No more in the midnight tempest
Will she mock the mounting sea,
Strong in her oaken timbers,
And her white sail’s ''bravery''.</poem>
{{right|''Halleck'', Epistles.}}}}
'''3†.''' Show; ostentation; parade.
{{smaller block|Prefaces, . . . and other speeches of reference to the person, are great wastes of time; and though they seem to proceed of modesty, they are ''bravery''. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor would I you should melt away yourself
In flashing ''bravery''.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, i. 1.}}}}
'''4†.''' Bravado; boast.
{{smaller block|I commended but their wits, madam, and their ''braveries''. I never looked toward their valours.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|There are those that make it a point of ''bravery'' to bid defiance to the oracles of divine revelation.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}
'''5†.''' A showy person.
{{smaller block|A man that is the ''bravery'' of his age. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.''}}}}
{{smaller block|He is one of the ''braveries'', though he be none of the wits.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn. 1.''' Valor, daring, pluck, boldness, mettle, audacity. For comparison, see ''brave''.}}

'''bravi''' (brä′vē). See remarks under ''bravo, interj.''

'''braving†''' (brā′ving), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''brave, v.'']   Bravado; defiance.
{{smaller block|With so proud a straine of threats and ''bravings.''
{{right|''Chapman'', Odyssey, xxi.}}}}

'''bravingly''' (brā′ving-li), ''adv.'' In a braving or defying manner.   ''Sheldon.'' [Rare.]

'''bravissimo''' (brä-vis′i-mō), ''interj.''   [It., superl. of ''bravo'', q. v.]   Superlative of ''bravo''.
{{smaller block|That’s right—I’m steel—Bravo!—Adamant—''Bravissimo!''
{{right|''Colman'', Jealous Wife, i. 1.}}}}

'''bravity†''', ''n.''   [< ''brave'' + ''-ity''.]   Bravery.

'''bravo''' (brä′vō), ''interj.''   [It. adj. (pl. ''bravi'', fem. ''brava'', pl. ''brave''), > F. ''brave'', > E. ''brave'', q. v.]   Well done! good! sometimes used as a noun: as, “with ''bravo'' and handclapping,” ''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. v. 6.
{{smaller block|The Italian Prima Donna sweeps a courtesy of careless pity to the over-facile pit which unsexes her with the ''bravo!''
{{right|''Lowell'', On a Certain Condescension in Foreigners.}}}}
{{smaller block|[In Italian the word is an adjective, and the correct usage is to say ''bravo'' to a male singer or actor, ''brava'' to a female, and ''bravi'' to a company; but in French and properly in English the word is a mere interjection. Careful persons familiar with the Italian usage do, however, discriminate as to gender.]}}

'''bravo''' (brä′vō), ''n.''; pl. ''bravos'' or ''bravoes'' (-vōz).   [It. (ML. ''bravus''), < ''bravo'', adj.: see ''brave''.]   A daring villain; a bandit; one who sets law at defiance; an assassin or murderer.
{{smaller block|<poem>Stab, like ''bravoes'', all who come that way.</poem>
{{right|''Churchill'', The Apology.}}}}
{{smaller block|Was not this Venice, and is not Venice forever associated with ''bravoes'' and unexpected dagger thrusts?
{{right|''Howells'', Venetian Life, xi.}}}}

'''bravura''' (brȧ-vö′rä), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [It., bravery, spirit, < ''bravo'': see ''brave.'']   '''I.''' ''n.'' In ''music'', a florid air, requiring great force and spirit in the performer, and serving to display his or her power, flexibility of voice, and distinctness of articulation.

'''II.''' ''a.'' In ''music'', spirited; florid; brilliant: as, a ''bravura'' air: chiefly applied to vocal compositions, but occasionally to instrumental.

'''braw''' (brâ), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [Sc.: see ''brave.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Brave; fine; gay; handsome; pleasant; agreeable; worthy; excellent; stout: as, a ''braw'' new gown; a ''braw'' man; ''braw'' lads and bonny lasses. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|There’s ''braw'', ''braw'' lads on Yarrow braes.
{{right|''Burns'', Gala Water.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n. pl.'' One’s best apparel; finery.

'''brawd†''', ''v. t.'' See ''broud'', ''broid.''

'''brawdery†''', ''n.'' An obsolete variant of ''broidery.''

'''brawet''' (brou′et), ''n.'' A young eel. Also written ''brawat.'' [North. Eng.]

'''brawl<sup>1</sup>''' (brâl), ''v.''   [Early mod. E. also ''brall'', < ME. ''brallen'', cry out, vociferate, = D. ''brallen'', boast, = Dan. ''bralle'', jabber, chatter, = MHG. ''prālen'', G. ''prahlen'', boast, vaunt, flaunt; apparently identical with ME. ''brawlen'', ''braulen'', quarrel, W. ''brawl'', a boast, ''brolio'', boast, vaunt, ''bragal'', vociferate, etc. Cf. also F.
